Mining · Botswana

Baselines and land change on mining concessions in Botswana

A dated baseline of the land before a licence application, an expansion or a new pit, then a record of what changes on and around the concession between dates. We map pits, disturbed ground, spoil, water-filled excavations, tracks, cleared ground and new structures, for diamond and copper leases, industrial-mineral and river-sand permits and sites under care and maintenance. Satellite first, your own drone imagery where you already fly, and a person reviews every result.

Send us your licence boundary See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Concessions are large, and the ground on them keeps changing

“The application needs the land described.”

A mining licence application needs surface rights from the land authority or landowner “with a stamped sketch plan showing coordinates”, authorisation of the environmental impact assessment by the Department of Environmental Affairs, archaeological clearance with location coordinates and, inside a conservation area, clearance from the Department of Wildlife and National Parks, together with a proposed rehabilitation programme (gov.bw).

“Is sand being dug outside the permitted stretches?”

The Minister of Minerals and Energy told Parliament in March 2026 that river systems “have been adversely impacted by over mining”, that no river sand is mined south of Dibete under a moratorium, extended to the Mahalapye area in 2025, and that permits along the Mahalapye River are being reopened after a study by the Botswana Geoscience Institute (Committee of Supply speech, 4 March 2026).

“The expansion needs a footprint record first.”

The same speech reports underground development at diamond mines, copper expansions that open new mines beside existing ones, and manganese, graphite and iron projects at different stages. Each new pit, haul road, camp and dump takes land, and the land needs a dated record before the census and compensation start.

“Nobody has walked the whole lease this year.”

Lease areas are large, and some include game parks. New tracks, cleared ground and structures at the edge, or pits opening inside it, are found on the next visit if they are found at all.

Who this is for

  • Mine land and surface-rights managers
  • Environmental, rehabilitation and closure managers
  • Community-relations teams
  • Holders of industrial-mineral and river-sand permits
  • Environmental assessment practitioners
  • Mine surveyors and geomatics teams, as users
  • Land authorities and inspectors
  • Lenders’ environmental and social advisers

Before the licence or the expansion

A baseline of the land, dated and reviewed

Environmental assessment in Botswana starts with a project brief to the Department of Environmental Affairs, which decides whether no further study, an environmental management plan or a full assessment is needed. The practitioner then publicises the activity in the media, in the official languages, for at least 21 days, holds meetings with the affected communities, and submits a scoping report before the assessment itself; the application’s supporting documents include proof of land ownership, such as a prospecting licence (gov.bw).

For each of those steps we give your practitioner and land team the same dated picture of the licence area and the ground around it: a land-use and land-cover map of built-up land, cropland, bare ground, water and tree cover, a layer of the structures on it with coordinates and IDs, and the imagery history of what was built, cleared or dug before, and roughly when. Reviewers mark structures by hand where roofs are hard to read, and categorise them as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction when a resettlement register is needed.

We are not an environmental assessment practitioner, and we do not do archaeological or heritage surveys. The baseline supports those who do.

What you receive

  • A land-use and land-cover baseline of the licence area and a ring around it
  • A structure layer with IDs, coordinates and reviewer categories
  • The imagery history of the area, with the date of every scene used
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Pits, sand and disturbed ground

Where the ground has been dug since the last survey

We map pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations inside and around your licence or permit area, and along the river stretches you name, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer. In the rainy season, radar comparisons show larger ground changes even under cloud, and flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or a drone check. New tracks and access roads into the area are mapped the same way, because they often come first.

The Minister says the Mines and Minerals (Amendment) Act, 2024, enacted in October 2025 and now in force, “had brought revised punitive measures and fees to deter those who were tempted to undertake illegal mining”, and that the Ministry is committed to the forfeiture of equipment used in it; the Ministry and other stakeholders run random and joint inspections (BOPA, 25 August 2026). A dated map of new excavations shows your teams and the inspectors where to look first. It is an indication to check, not proof of who did anything.

Small concessions. A minerals permit covers a concession of no more than 0.5 km² for minerals other than diamonds, and permits for industrial minerals are reserved for citizens unless the Minister decides otherwise in the public interest (gov.bw). For a permit holder, the same map shows whether digging has spread beyond the permitted area.

Concession oversight, in the Ministry’s words

As part of optimised regulation of small mines, the Ministry of Minerals and Energy plans “to increase monitoring of concessions through the use of new technology such as drones”, which it says can also give feedback on “the actual amount of material that has been mined” (Committee of Supply speech, 4 March 2026).

We map the extent of disturbed ground between dates from satellite imagery, and calculate volumes from drone elevation models where they exist. Volumes are indicative, not certified.

Land, never people

What we map is the ground. We do not identify, count or follow people, and underground workings and covered shafts are not visible from above.

Lease boundaries and zones

What stands inside your concession, and in a ring around it

Structures by boundary and ring

Each structure inside the licence area and in the ring you choose around it, with its distance to the boundary, so land and community teams see where settlement meets the concession.

Tracks, clearing and new structures

New tracks, cleared ground and new structures at the boundary between dates, with fence lines and gates checked by a reviewer on drone imagery. Fences are too thin to find on satellite imagery.

Zones your engineers define

The structures inside the blast, tailings and safety zones you supply, each with its distance to the source, and how that list changes between surveys. We list what stands there; we do not model the zones.

When a pit, dump or haul road expands, we record the structures inside the new footprint on a date you fix. Where lenders apply IFC Performance Standard 5, people who move into the project area after a cut-off date that “has been clearly established and made public” need not be compensated (PS5, para. 23), so the dated register supports the census and asset inventory. It does not replace them, and its categories do not establish use, ownership or value.

Rehabilitation, care and maintenance

Dated evidence of rehabilitation, and of what happens on quiet sites

Every mining licence application carries a proposed rehabilitation programme. We track revegetation on rehabilitated land between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data and, where flown, drone elevation models, and compare cut and fill between drone visits. That shows the trend; it is not an ecological assessment or a closure sign-off.

The Minister’s March 2026 speech lists mines under care and maintenance or in liquidation, and shafts that have been backfilled. Sites without daily operations change too: we flag new excavations, structures and tracks on them between dates, so the owner, the liquidator or the Ministry knows what to inspect.

Vegetation, land cover and fire · Excavation mapping

Your drone imagery, and drone surveys

Drones on and around mine sites

We found no drone rule specific to mines in Botswana. The general rules apply: the Civil Aviation (Remotely Piloted Aircraft) Regulations, 2024 require the consent of “the relevant Authority” to launch or recover a drone from any public or private property (reg. 100), CAAB’s checklist asks commercial operators for the property owner’s letter of authorisation, and each commercial operation needs its own CAAB authorisation, including a security review of how the camera will be used. Where a lease area takes in a game park or wildlife sanctuary, CAAB’s 2016 bye-law, whose status after 2024 is to be confirmed with CAAB, bars flights over national game parks and wildlife sanctuaries, and over wildlife in a way that may disturb it, so it may apply there too.

If your survey team already flies the mine, send the orthophotos and we run the analysis on them. New drone surveys are subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

Drone law in Botswana

Ownership and registration, the RPAS Operator Certificate, security vetting, the flight limits and a checklist for clients, last reviewed 27 September 2026.

How it works

From licence boundary to reviewed map

  1. Scope

    You send the licence or permit boundary, the buffer or zones you want reported, the river stretches that matter and what the record is for: an application, an expansion, inspections or closure. We agree the imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Baseline

    A dated baseline of land cover, structures and existing excavations, from satellite imagery, open datasets or your own orthophotos.

  3. Re-survey

    The area is compared again on the schedule you agree with us, and new pits, spoil, tracks and structures are flagged automatically.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result before the report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name, with a notice of what changed.

More on how it works, the methodology, imagery and data sources and our global mining page.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map pits, spoil, water-filled excavations, tracks and cleared ground visible from the air
  • List structures inside your concession, a ring around it and the zones you define
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Analyse the drone imagery you already fly

What we don’t do

  • Identify, count or follow people
  • See underground workings, or verify title and surface rights
  • Certify volumes, or model blasts and tailings failures
  • Replace the environmental assessment, the archaeological clearance or the census

Frequently asked questions

Can you tell us who is digging on our concession?

No. We map the ground, such as pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations, disturbed ground and new tracks, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer. We never identify or count people, underground workings are not visible from above, and whether and how to act on a flagged site is for you and the authorities to decide.

Can you measure how much sand or ore has been removed?

Satellite imagery shows how far disturbed ground has spread between dates, not its depth. Volumes of pits, spoil heaps and stockpiles come from drone elevation models, where a drone survey is flown or you supply one, and they are indicative for your own planning, not certified quantities.

Can your baseline replace the surface-rights plan or the EIA?

No. The surface rights and their stamped sketch plan come from the land authority or landowner, the environmental authorisation from the Department of Environmental Affairs, and the archaeological clearance from the Department of National Museum and Monuments. Our land-use and structure baseline is an input for your environmental assessment practitioner and your land team, not a substitute for any of them.

Can you confirm our licence boundary?

No. We work from the coordinates you give us and do not verify title or surface rights. Licence areas are administered by the Ministry of Minerals and Energy, whose Botswana Mining Cadastre System went live on 1 November 2022; where a boundary needs to be surveyed or beaconed, that is a land surveyor’s work.

Does satellite monitoring of our lease need a drone permit?

No aircraft is flown, so no CAAB approval is involved. We found no Botswana law restricting the analysis of commercial satellite imagery; counsel should confirm it for your project. Drone detail, where you want it, is planned separately and is subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

We already fly our own drones. Can you use that imagery?

Yes. Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs your survey team already produces and we run the same excavation, structure and boundary analysis on them, with a reviewer confirming every result. Results depend on the imagery’s resolution and quality, which we check on a sample first.

Send us the licence or permit boundary

Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON, the kind of licence or permit, the district, any buffer or zone you want reported, and what you already fly. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
